hub.description: Decks and fences for Nashville, TN homes on small lots with close neighbors, where alley access and historic overlay review shape the plan.
hub.intro: Behind many Nashville houses, the backyard is narrow and the house next door is only a few steps away. When homeowners in the older parts of town start thinking about a fence or a deck, privacy is usually the first thing they bring up. Access comes next, because many lots are reached by an alley or by a side yard barely wide enough for a wheelbarrow. On some streets, a historic or conservation overlay adds its own review. Below is a short overview of both services in Nashville, with links to the deck and fence pages when you want more detail.

sections.heading: Close neighbors and small backyards
paragraphs: In East Nashville, Germantown, and 12 South, many houses sit on narrow lots with side yards you can cross in a few steps. Newer infill homes, often two stories, now stand beside older bungalows, and their back windows can look straight down into the yard next door. That is a big part of why privacy tops the list for so many Nashville homeowners. It shapes deck plans too, since a deck raised well off the ground puts you on display unless screening is part of the design.

In a small yard, every bit of open ground has a job. Cover all of it with a deck and there is nowhere left for the dog or a garden bed. A fence run tight against a neighbor's house can leave them no way to paint or repair that wall later. Before picking a deck size or a fence line, think about how the yard gets used on an ordinary weekday. Sometimes a low deck and one tall stretch of fence do more for privacy than a big structure.

sections.heading: Alleys and narrow side yards
paragraphs: Plenty of older Nashville streets have alleys behind the houses, and that usually helps. Posts and lumber can come in from the back instead of being carried past the house. Alleys come with their own things to work around, though, like overhead lines and neighbors who need to get their cars through. Where there is no alley, every board goes through the side yard by hand, which takes longer. Mention how your lot is reached when you [request an estimate](#estimate), since it affects the plan and the price.

sections.heading: Historic and conservation overlays
paragraphs: Some Nashville neighborhoods sit inside historic or conservation zoning overlays, and those overlays can review changes to the outside of a house. What gets reviewed depends on the type of overlay, so a fence that needs approval on one street may not need it on another. Metro requires a preservation permit for a fence in a historic preservation or landmark overlay, but not in a neighborhood conservation overlay. Before you settle on a design, ask the Metro Historic Zoning Commission staff about your address. Their review is its own step, separate from the building permit, and it can add time.

Most permits here run through the Metro Codes office, since Nashville and Davidson County share one government. A few small cities inside the county keep their own rules, and Belle Meade is one of them. If your address falls inside one of those cities, expect the permit and any design review to go through that city instead. Rules on fence height and deck placement vary from place to place, so confirm what applies to your lot before work is scheduled.

sections.heading: Decks for Nashville homes
paragraphs: Nashville deck projects tend to start from one of a few places. Older bungalows often have a worn back deck or porch that has been patched more than once. Infill houses frequently come with a small landing and a back door set well above the yard. In Bellevue and other hilly parts of Nashville, the ground can drop away behind the house, which means taller posts and a longer stair. Limestone also sits close to the surface in many yards, so footing holes sometimes hit rock early. The [Nashville deck builder page](/deck-builder-nashville-tn/) goes through all of this in more detail.

sections.heading: Fences for Nashville yards
paragraphs: Most fence conversations in Nashville come back to privacy along the side and rear lines. A solid wood privacy fence is the usual answer, with a gate facing the alley if the lot has one. Bigger lots in Donelson and Belle Meade raise other questions, like a longer run with more than one gate, or keeping posts away from the roots of large trees. On any Nashville lot, the property line needs to be settled before a post goes in, and our guide on [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) explains why. The [Nashville fence page](/fence-company-nashville-tn/) covers the rest.

faqs.q: How do I find out if my Nashville house is in a historic or conservation overlay?
faqs.a: Metro Nashville publishes property maps online that show the zoning on each parcel, including overlays. The Metro Historic Zoning Commission staff can also tell you whether your address is covered and what they review there. Ask before you pick a fence style or a deck location, not after. If the house is in an overlay, have a simple drawing ready that shows where the project goes and what it will look like, since it makes the conversation with staff much quicker.

faqs.q: Our house is in Belle Meade. Does Metro handle the permit?
faqs.a: Not always. Belle Meade is its own city inside Davidson County, with its own rules for building and zoning. If your address is within the city of Belle Meade, check with that city's office about permits and any design review for a deck or fence. Some addresses near Belle Meade are still in Metro Nashville, so the mailing address alone may not settle it. The property maps or a quick call will tell you which office covers your lot.

faqs.q: Our backyard is tiny. Is it worth adding both a deck and a fence?
faqs.a: Often it is, as long as the two are planned together. On a small Nashville lot, a low deck off the back door and a privacy fence along the sides can make the yard feel like a room you actually use. Planning both at once lets the gate and the deck stairs fit around each other instead of fighting for the same few feet of ground. If the budget covers only one this year, say so, and the second can be planned now and built later.

deck.description: Deck builder in Nashville, TN for small backyards beside tall infill homes, with historic overlay review and Metro permits sorted out early.
deck.intro: A deck in Nashville usually has to fit a tight space. Yards in the older neighborhoods are small, and the neighbor's windows are rarely far away. Your house might be an older bungalow over a low crawl space, or a new infill build whose back door sits well above the ground. On some streets, historic review is an extra step on top of the Metro permit. It pays to plan around those limits first and settle size and materials after that. The sections below answer what homeowners here tend to ask before they hire a deck builder.

sections.heading: Sizing a deck for a small Nashville backyard
paragraphs: Many lots in Sylvan Park and 12 South leave little open ground once the house and a parking pad are in. A deck that fills the whole yard can look good on paper, then the dog has no grass and there is no spot for a garden bed. Before choosing a size, mark the outline on the ground with string or spray paint and walk around inside it. Picture the grill and the table in place, with room to pull the chairs out.

Setbacks from the side and rear lines matter more on a narrow Nashville lot. Metro zoning limits how close a deck can sit to the property line, and those limits change with the zoning of your lot, so ask the codes office before the design is final. A low deck close to the ground is often the easiest fit. It needs only a short stair and keeps you below the top of a privacy fence.

sections.heading: Privacy when the house next door is taller
paragraphs: When a two story infill house goes up beside your Nashville home, its upstairs windows may look straight down at your deck. A fence helps at ground level but does little for a raised deck. Screening built into the deck frame does more. That might be a run of solid boards on the side facing the neighbor, a slatted wall that lets the breeze through, or a pergola with partial cover overhead. Screens catch wind, so their posts need to tie firmly into the framing. A tall screen can also raise zoning or overlay questions, so check before you commit.

Placement can solve part of the problem before any screen is built. Moving the deck to the side of the house away from the neighbor's windows, or keeping it low and close to the back wall, often cuts the view more than adding height to a railing. Some lots have only one or two workable spots, and it helps to stand in each of them at different times of day before deciding.

sections.heading: Older houses in East Nashville and Germantown
paragraphs: Houses in the older parts of East Nashville and Germantown were not built with a deck in mind. Many sit over a crawl space, and the wood a deck would bolt to may be old or softened by years of water from a leaky gutter. When an old deck comes off, it is common to find rot behind it where water was trapped against the house. If the house framing is sound, a new deck can attach to it with proper flashing. Where it is not, a freestanding deck on its own posts, set just off the wall, is often the safer choice.

Siding matters as well. Older houses may have wood lap siding or brick, and some have vinyl laid over the original boards. Each calls for a different way of attaching and sealing the ledger. Opening up a small patch of siding where the deck will meet the house, before the plan is final, can head off a surprise on the first day of work.

sections.heading: Historic review for a Nashville deck
paragraphs: If your Nashville house sits inside a historic or conservation overlay, Metro Codes tells deck applicants to contact the historic zoning staff about any rules that apply. Ask early, before the design is final. Where review applies, it may look at where the deck sits, how large it is next to the house, and whether it covers original features like a back porch. Our guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the permit side in general terms.

sections.heading: Permits and inspections through Metro Codes
paragraphs: Building a new deck or replacing an old one in Nashville takes a permit from the Metro Codes office, and the work is inspected along the way, often starting with the footing holes before concrete goes in. A deck built without a permit can cause trouble later, because buyers' inspectors and lenders tend to ask about it when you sell. Belle Meade handles its own permits, as do some other small cities inside Davidson County. Ask any deck builder you talk to who pulls the permit and whether the fee is included in the bid.

sections.heading: Digging footings in the Nashville Basin
paragraphs: Nashville sits in a basin where limestone lies close to the surface in many yards. A footing hole can go down easily at one corner and hit a ledge of rock at the next. The fix is to drill or break the rock, or shift the post layout so the footings land where digging works. Between the ledges there is often dense clay that stays wet after a rain and cracks during a dry summer. Footings need to bear on firm, undisturbed soil or rock, never on loose fill.

Hillier parts of Nashville bring slope into the picture. In Bellevue, a lot can fall away from the house fast enough to turn a simple deck into one standing well above the grade, with taller posts and a longer stair. Near the Harpeth River, or along creeks elsewhere in the county, check the flood map for your lot first, since building in a floodplain can bring extra rules. Mention the slope when you [ask for an estimate](#estimate).

faqs.q: Can a real deck replace the small landing on my Nashville infill house?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Many newer infill homes come with a back landing just big enough to open the door, sitting well above the yard. A deck can replace it or grow out from it, but that height means taller posts and a longer stair. It helps to know how the landing was attached to the house, so ask the builder or check the plans if you have them. If your house shares a lot with a second home, read the shared agreement before planning anything in the yard.

faqs.q: Do I need historic approval for a deck behind my house in Germantown?
faqs.a: It depends on whether your lot is inside an overlay and what that overlay covers. Look up your parcel on the Metro Nashville property maps, or call the historic zoning staff and give them your address. If review applies, do not assume a rear deck is exempt just because it sits behind the house. Get a clear answer before the permit application goes in, since starting over later costs time.

faqs.q: What decking holds up under the big shade trees in older Nashville neighborhoods?
faqs.a: Heavy shade keeps a deck cooler, but it also keeps it damp. Wood under old trees tends to grow mildew and collect leaves in the gaps between boards, so it needs regular cleaning and a sealer suited to shade. Composite resists rot better than wood but can still get slick with mildew. In a sunny infill yard with no trees, surface heat on the boards becomes the bigger question. Our [guide to wood and composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) compares them in more detail.

faqs.q: I rent out my Nashville house or a back cottage. What kind of deck makes sense for guests?
faqs.a: Guests tend to be rougher on a deck than owners are, and nobody sweeps the leaves off between stays. Simple layouts hold up best, with sturdy railings and a stair that is easy to see at night. Choose boards that clean up quickly between bookings. A hot tub on the deck is a much heavier load and a bigger project, so raise it at the start and ask Metro Codes what the permit will need.

faqs.q: What should I ask a Nashville deck builder before signing?
faqs.a: Start with who pulls the Metro permit and whether handling historic review, if your street needs it, is part of the job. Rock is another good topic, since a footing that hits limestone can change the price. Get the board type and railing style in writing. On a lot with no alley, find out how materials will reach the backyard and what happens to the old deck when it comes off. A clear bid makes it easier to compare deck builders side by side.

fence.description: Fence installation in Nashville, TN: privacy fences for close neighbors and alley lots, with overlay review and the property line checked first.
fence.intro: Ask Nashville homeowners why they want a fence and most will say privacy. Houses in the older neighborhoods stand close together, and new infill homes have put taller walls and more windows along many side lines. A well built privacy fence will not block every view, but it can make a small yard feel like yours again. This page covers what fence installation in Nashville involves on a narrow lot, and what changes when your street has historic review.

sections.heading: Privacy fences for close neighbors in Nashville
paragraphs: Along a side line in East Nashville or 12 South, the fence may run only a few steps from the neighbor's wall. A solid style such as board on board covers the gaps that open up as boards dry and shrink, which matters when the next house is that close. Horizontal slat fences are common beside newer infill homes, though they usually need closer post spacing so the boards do not sag. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares the common styles.

Height is where most people run into limits. Metro Nashville zoning sets how tall a fence can be, and the answer can differ between the front yard and the back, or inside an overlay. Confirm the allowed height for your lot first, then pick a style that makes good use of it. A fence built taller than your lot allows may have to be cut down or taken out later.

sections.heading: Alley lots and back gates
paragraphs: When your Nashville lot backs onto an alley, the rear fence line becomes the main way in and out of the yard. Most homeowners with alley lots want a gate there, wide enough to roll a trash cart or a mower through. A gate facing an alley usually works best swinging into the yard, so it never blocks the alley or catches a passing car. Gate posts take more strain than any other posts on the fence, so they need deep holes and solid concrete. Look for overhead lines and poles along the alley too, and leave utility crews room to reach them.

sections.heading: Front yard fences on historic Nashville streets
paragraphs: Overlay type decides whether a Nashville fence gets historic review. In a historic preservation or landmark overlay, Metro requires a preservation permit for a fence. In a neighborhood conservation overlay, Metro says fencing does not need one. Either way, Metro zoning keeps solid fences low near the front of the lot, so a tall privacy fence usually belongs along the side and rear. Call the Metro Historic Zoning Commission staff with your address and a rough sketch before any materials are ordered.

sections.heading: Finding the line on a narrow Nashville lot
paragraphs: When the lot is narrow, being off by a few inches matters. Old fences in the older parts of Nashville may not sit on the true line, since some went up long ago without a survey. Find your corner pins, or have a surveyor mark them, before fence installation starts. Our guide on [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) explains why the line comes first and how to talk it over with a neighbor. Call Tennessee 811 before any digging so buried utility lines get marked.

Lots where two newer houses share one parcel add another wrinkle. Many of those pairs come with a shared agreement that spells out who controls which part of the yard, and some limit fences between the two homes. Read that document, and talk with the other owner, before planning a fence down the middle. It is much easier to settle this on paper than after posts are set.

sections.heading: Setting posts around rock and old tree roots
paragraphs: Limestone sits close to the surface in much of Nashville, and a post hole can stop short on a ledge. If it does, the hole can be drilled into the rock, or the post can move a little along the line if the spacing allows. Older Nashville neighborhoods add large tree roots, and sometimes buried brick or old concrete from an earlier structure. Keeping posts clear of major roots protects the tree as well as the fence. In the clay between the rock, posts set in concrete on firm ground hold their line best.

sections.heading: Bigger yards in Donelson and Bellevue
paragraphs: Not every Nashville yard is tiny. Donelson has many ranch houses on wider lots, and if yours still has old chain link around the back, replacing it with a privacy fence means a longer run and more gates to plan. Decide early whether the old fence comes out first or stays up until the new one is finished. With a dog in the yard, keeping the old fence in place a few extra days can save a lot of worry.

Bellevue, on the southwest side of Nashville, has hills along the Harpeth River and newer subdivisions, and some of those have HOAs that review fence style and color. On a slope, fence sections are either stepped down the hill or angled to follow it, and each leaves a different gap at the bottom. Lots near the Harpeth River may sit in a floodplain, where a solid fence can catch water and debris, so check the flood map before you choose a style. When you are ready, [request an estimate](#estimate) and tell us about the slope.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence in Nashville?
faqs.a: Metro Nashville does not currently require a permit for a residential fence, but the fence still has to meet zoning rules on height and placement, which differ between the front yard and the side and rear. If your home is in a historic preservation or landmark overlay, you need a preservation permit from the historic zoning staff. Belle Meade and some other small cities in the county set their own rules. A fence company that works in Nashville should help you sort this out before a contract is signed.

faqs.q: The neighbor's house sits right by our side line. Can the fence go there?
faqs.a: Often it can, but think it through first. A fence tight against their wall may leave them no way to paint or repair that side of the house without coming into your yard. Some homeowners add a gate in that stretch, and others set the fence slightly inside their own line to leave room. Talk with your neighbor before fence installation starts, and confirm where the line actually falls with your pins or a survey.

faqs.q: Will a privacy fence stop the people in the tall house next door from seeing our yard?
faqs.a: Not completely. A fence blocks the view at ground level and from most ground floor windows, but a window two or three floors up looks right over it. For those sight lines, a pergola over the patio or a tree planted in the right spot often does more. What a fence does well is give you privacy while you are sitting in the yard, which is where most people feel it. Stand out back and figure out which window bothers you before choosing a height.

faqs.q: Can our fence run right up to the alley?
faqs.a: Usually the fence follows your rear property line, and that line does not always match the edge of the alley pavement. Some lots stop short of the pavement, and others have poles or easements along the back. Check your survey first, then ask Metro Nashville whether any rules apply to fences along an alley on your street. Setting the gate back slightly from the alley also gives you room to step out without walking into traffic.

faqs.q: What should I ask a fence company in Nashville before I sign?
faqs.a: Find out whether the price assumes rock and what changes if post holes hit limestone. Ask who confirms the property line and who calls Tennessee 811. Put the style and height in writing, along with which side of the fence faces out and how many gates you are getting. If your house is in an overlay or an HOA, ask whether the company will prepare the drawings for review or expects you to. Clear answers make it much easier to compare bids.
